newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia continues move to real time settlement.
newsitem.headline: Australia continues move to real time settlement.

text.p: The Australian money market's progression to a real time settlement takes another step on Monday with the start of a "shadow" real time gross settlement (RTGS) system.
The move to a shadow system follows the opening on May 12 of the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) central test site environment, and RTGS is expected to be fully implemented in April 1998.

From Monday, banks will still settle at 9.00 a.m. (2300 GMT) the next day, but will be "shadow posting" to RTGS accounts, RBA chief manager of Financial System Department, John Veale, said a function on RTGS in late May.

RTGS is designed to reduce both settlement and systemic risk by requiring parties to have funds in their accounts when a transaction takes place, rather than clearing that transaction at the end of the day or the next day.
Veale described RTGS as a pretty fundamental reform to the payments and financial system, that would introduce a new philosphy for high value payments.
Funds must be in an account for the transaction to proceed, and once the transaction is made it is irrevocable

Under the system, if one party does not have the funds for a transaction, it is detected immediately and eliminates the risk of a default disrupting a chain of transactions, as could occur under the present settlement system.

Settlement risk on foreign exchange transactions, or Herstatt risk, could still be a problem due to the fact that there are time zone differences involved in the settlement of international transactions.
State Street Bank And Trust managing director Russell Kent said RTGS would significantly impact that way banks manage their daily liquidity requirements.

"One development may be the establishment of a 'middle' office, in addition to traditional 'front' and 'back' offices, to monitor and control particpants' real time cash positions," he said in a statement.
RTGS should provide a stronger and more stable platform for the payments system, with reduced interbank credit exposures and liquity risks for domestic markets," he said.

RTGS, because of the heavy demands it places on liquidity, will result in increased costs for banks that may be passed onto customers in transaction charges, especially for urgent payments early in the day, Kennett said.
